newsitem.title: USA: Quaker looks to put Snapple behind it.
newsitem.headline: Quaker looks to put Snapple behind it.

text.p: Quaker Oats Co. Chairman William Smithburg, who is expected to retire within a year, told shareholders Wednesday that the company must put its failed Snapple beverage acquisition behind it.
"Snapple clearly did not pan out," Smithburg said repeatedly at the annual meeting here.
Quaker bought Snapple more than two years ago in a deal worth $1.8 billion, hoping to build on the success of its Gatorade sports drink. The gains never materialised.

Quaker Oats took a $1.1 billion write-off for Snapple in the first quarter after agreeing to sell the fruit-flavored beverage and iced tea business for $300 million. Coupled with $250 million in recouped taxes, the Snapple sale to Triarc Cos. will bring in about $550 million.
Asked if he wished Quaker had never bought Snapple, Smithburg said, "At this point in time (Quaker must) look forward."

Smithburg faced some criticism for Snapple at the otherwise low-keyed annual meeting. One shareholder demanded to see the "fairness" reports that were prepared by investment bankers to analyse the purchase price for Snapple and the final deal to sell it.
The shareholder was later told that his request would be taken under advisement.

The key to the future for Quaker, Smithburg said, will be its U.S. and Canadian foods businesses, with brands like Cap'n Crunch and Life cereal and Rice-a-Roni rice dishes, that account for about 70 percent of its profit.
Gatorade worldwide accounts for another 30 percent of profits. Smithburg predicted that Gatorade sales this year will be about $1.5 billion, up from $1.4 billion in 1996.
Quaker's annual sales, excluding Snapple, are about $5 billion.

In the second quarter, which includes the start of the so-called beverage season, Gatorade will face a tough comparison with the 1996 period, which benefited from hot weather. Gatorade's sales in the 1996 second quarter were up 14 percent.

"So that's a tough nut to go against," James Doyle, executive vice president who is in charge of Gatorade, told reporters after the annual meeting. "But I think the sales will come through. We've got very good momentum on the brand."
One positive development is Gatorade's new "Frost" line, which could account for 10 to 20 percent of U.S. sales for the sports drink, Doyle said,
He added that Frost, sold only in the United States, is pitched for individual sports, whereas traditional Gatorade is linked to team competition such as basketball and football.

While he later told reporters "the Snapple era" is behind the company, the failed business venture came at the end of Smithburg's 31-year career at the Chicago-based food company, including 16 years as chief executive officer.
Smithburg said in April he planned to retire, adding an executive search firm has been hired to find a successor. He said candidates inside and outside the company would be considered.
Smithburg said he to retire before next year's annual meeting. Asked what he intended to do, Smithburg, 58, said, "I'm retiring from Quaker, but not from life."
